full_judgment:
3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement. He denied the plaintiffs' case and asserted that the suit land originally belonged to one Mahesh Chandra Chakroborty who sold the same to Ram Sundar Saha. Ram Sundar Saha leased out the suit land to Jamiruddin, Golam Nabi and Minnat Ali who in their turn sold the same to Pitamber by kabala dated 26 Chaitra, 1304 B.S. Ext. B(1). Pitamber died leaving 3 sons from whom the property devolved upon Raj Mohan and others by inheritance. They exchanged their lands including the suit land with defendant No. 1 by a deed of exchange dated 22.2.64 (Ext. B) Defendant 1 is in possession of the suit land by virtue of the said exchange and asserted that the M.R.R. Khatian was correctly prepared in the names of his vendors. 

 The learned Munsif upon a consideration of the evidence (on remand) found that the plaintiffs failed to prove that defendants No 4 to 6 are the heirs of Samad Ali, that they failed to adduce any material evidence to show that Samad Ali's tenancy was ever continued, that the plaintiffs created some documents in collusion with defendants 2-6 taking advantage of the entry in the khatian Ext. 3 when Samad Ali had no title and possession, that the Dakhilas Ext. 2(a) 2(c) were not genuine and thus the plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief. The learned Munsif, however, found that Pitambar and after his death his heirshad been possessing the suitland and that there was no reason to disbelieve the defendant's case of exchange based on documents Accordingly the suit was dismissed. 

 5. On appeal by the plaintiffs the learned Subordinate Judge, Additional Court, Noakhali allowed the appeal and decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs sufficiently proved their title and possession in the suit land. As regards defendant's case it was found on the basis of Ext. 3 and B(1) that Jamiruddin, Golam Nabi and Minnat Ali had taluki right in the suit property and they sold their taluki interest by kabla Ext. B(1) to Pitambar, that the vendors of defendant No. 1 had accordingly inherited taluki right from Pitambar which was acquired by the Government under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act since 1956 and consequently defendant No. 1 cannot claim rioytiright and Khas Possession in the suit land on the basis of exchange (Ext. B). 

 7. Leave was granted to consider two questions: (1) whether the tenancy of Samad Ali continued in the facts and circumstances of the case as found by the Subordinate Judge and (2) Whether the kabala Ext. B(1) has been properly construed by him. 

 8. Mr. M.H. Khondker, learned counsel for the appellants, argued that there being no evidence as to the existence of Samad Ali's tenancy beyond the limited period as mentioned in the khatian Ext. 3 and the rent receipts Ext. 2 series belatedly produced by the plaintiffs having been found to be spurious by the trial court, the Subordinate Judge acted illegally in holding that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary it is presumed that Samad Ali was tenant in respect of the suit property and his right continued. Mr. Khandker upon placing the recitals of kabala Ext. B(1) submitted that it was abundantly clear that Jamir Ali and others did not only sell taluki interest in the suit land as wrongly held by the learned Subordinate Judge but as a matter of fact they sold their khash right in the property. Mr. Khandker submitted that the learned Judge of the High Court Division also failed to appreciate correctly the documents Ext. 3 and B (1) and thus illegally endorsedthe findings made by the Subordinate Judge. 

 9. Mr. Nurul Hoque, learned Counsel for the plaintiff respondents while supporting the findings made by the learned Subordinate Judge, submitted with force that the plaintiffs having been found to be in possession of the suit land the possessory title of the plaintiffs' vendors in any case was there notwithstanding the entry as to the limited right of tenancy of Samad Ali in Ext. 3. 

 10. Khatian (Ext. 3) was prepared in 1893-94 showing Samad Ali as the tenant and it was also recorded ( দখলী স্বত্ব শুন্য ৮ বৎসর). The learned Munsif found that the plaintiffs completely failed to adduce any material evidence to show that Samad Ali's tenancy continued. He also noticed that the plaintiff is silent as to landlord of Samad Ali. He observed that it was only after the remand of the suit that the plaintiffs filed some spurious dakhilas Ex. 2(a) - 2(c) allegedly granted by Pitamber. Admittedly the M.R.R. Khatian (Ext.c) is in the name of the successors of Pitamber and the learned Munsif found from Ext. D that it was decided by A.S.O. in 1959 that the predecessors of the plaintiffs had no possession in the suit land. Pitamber's heirs paid rent Ext. F to F(a). The learned Munsif noticed that P.W. 1 admitted that he did not ever see Samad Ali, that his evidence as to possession of Samad Ali could not, therefore be relied upon and no other P.Ws. said anything as regards possession of the suit land by Samad Ali. Considering all these oral and documentary evidence and circumstances the learned Munsif found that Pitamber and after his death his heirs had been possessing the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge, it is found, altogether ignored the aforesaid material facts & documents and abruptly held without any basis that it is presumed that Samad Ali's tenancy right continued. Similarly his finding as to plaintiffs' possession suffers from non-consideration of aforesaid material documents & the important fact that there is no evidence of possession of the plaintiffs' predecessors right from the beginning of the present century upto 1963 when the plaintiffs allegedly purchased. Thus both the findings as to continuance of Samad Ali's tenancy and plaintiffs' possession are open to question and cannot be legally sustained. 

 13. In view of the discussion above it must be said that the lower appellate court and the learned Judge of the High Court Division committed substantial error in holding that tenancy of Samad Ali continued and that under Ext. B(1) the Taluki interest only was transferred to Pitamber and this error has resulted in wrong decision in the case. Furthermore, the important finding of the trial court, which seems to be correct, that defendants 4-6 are not the heirs of Samad Ali has not been properly reversed. Consequently, in any view of the matter, the suit could not be decreed.
